'''''Mollugo verticillata''''',<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?101375|title=Taxonomy - GRIN-Global Web v 1.9.8.2|website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|access-date=2016-11-03}}</ref> the '''green carpetweed'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=MOVE|taxon=Mollugo verticillata|accessdate=13 July 2015}}</ref> (also known as '''Indian chickweed'''<ref>{{cite journal |author-last=Bergen|author-first=Fanny D.|author-link=Fanny Dickerson Bergen |title=Popular American Plant-Names|journal=The Journal of American Folklore|publisher=American Folklore Society|volume=5|issue=17 |date=1892|pages=89–106 |doi=10.2307/533542 |jstor=533542|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1431369 |language=en|doi-access=free}}</ref>), is a rapidly spreading [[annual plant]] from tropical [[Americas|America]]. In eastern [[North America]], it is a common [[weed]] growing in disturbed areas. It forms a prostrate circular mat that can quickly climb over nearby plants and obstacles. The species has been reported from every state in the United States except Alaska, Hawaii, and Utah, as well as from British Columbia, Manitoba. Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.<ref name=vert/>  Although considered an invasive weed, ''M. verticillata'' is also known to be edible. Archaeological evidence has shown that  ''M. verticillata'' has been in North America for about 3000 years. Sometimes also referred to as "Indian chickweed", in China this plant is referred to as ''zhong leng su mi cao''.

==Description==
Carpetweed has narrow, [[Whorl (botany)|whorled]] leaves, 3-8 at each [[Node (botany)|node]].  At maturity the plant may lose its characteristic [[basal rosette]] formation. Leaves are approximately 1–3 cm in length and possess an [[Glossary of leaf morphology|obovate]] shape. Leaf apex may vary from rounded to acute.<ref name=vert>{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220008715|title=''Mollugo verticillata'' |series= Flora of North America|website=efloras.org|access-date=2016-12-03}}</ref> Due to its habit of prostrate growth, the plant will grow and sprawl across the soil and form mats.<ref name=health>{{Cite journal|last1=Ferreira|first1=A. P.|last2=Soares|first2=G. L. G.|last3=Salgado|first3=C. A.|last4=Gonçalves|first4=L. S.|last5=Teixeira|first5=F. M.|last6=Teixeira|first6=H. C.|last7=Kaplan|first7=M. A. C.|date=2003-01-01|title=Immunomodulatory activity of ''Mollugo verticillata'' L.|journal=Phytomedicine|volume=10|issue=2|pages=154–158|doi=10.1078/094471103321659861|pmid=12725569}}</ref> The flowers are usually in clusters of 2-5, blooming from July through September. Flowers are white or greenish white with tiny 5–15 mm stalks. Flowers quickly turn into fruit that is egg shaped and 1.5–4 mm in length. The dehiscent capsule opens at maturity. The seeds are 0.5 mm long and are red to rusty brown in coloration.<ref>{{cite journal|author=D'Arcy, W.G. |year=1987|title= Flora of Panama. Checklist and Index. Part 1: The introduction and checklist|journal= Monographs in Systematic Botany from the Missouri Botanical Garden |volume=17}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=P. D. Strausbaugh |name-list-style=and |author2=Earl L. Core|title=Flora of West Virginia |edition=2nd |publisher= Seneca Books Inc.|year= 1964|isbn=0-89092-010-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Richard H. Uva|author2= Joseph C. Neal|name-list-style= and |author3=Joseph M. Ditomaso|title= Weeds of the Northeast|publisher= Cornell University Press|year= 1997|isbn=0-8014-8334-4}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Advances in molecular genetic sequencing have improved understanding of the taxonomic relationship in the family Molluginaceae, which had previously not been as inclusive.<ref name=isolated>{{Cite journal|last1=Schäferhoff|first1=Bastian|last2=Müller|first2=Kai|last3=Borsch|first3=Thomas|title=Caryophyllales phylogenetics: disentangling Phytolaccaceae and Molluginaceae and description of Microteaceae as a new isolated family|journal=Willdenowia|volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=209–228|doi=10.3372/wi.39.39201|year=2009|doi-access=free |bibcode=2009Willd..39..209S }}</ref> Genera from Molluginaceae had previously been placed under Aizoaceae, Nyctaginaceae, and Phytolaccaceae before recent studies.<ref name= family>{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=20193|title=Molluginaceae|series= Flora of North America|website=efloras.org|access-date=2016-11-03}}</ref> The genus ''Mollugo'' [[Taxonomic authority|L.]] currently comprises about 35 species of annual herbs.<ref name=herbarium>{{Cite web|url=http://herbarium.unc.edu/flora.htm|title=UNC Herbarium|website=herbarium.unc.edu|access-date=2016-10-30}}</ref> Several subtaxa species of ''M. verticillata'' have been reported due to its varying morphological nature; however, they are not thoroughly documented.<ref name=vert /> ''Mollugo'' ''verticillata'' has many accepted synonyms, including ''Mollugo dichotoma'', ''Mollugo diffusa'', ''Mollugo costata'', ''Pharnaceum arenarium,'' and ''Pharnaceum verticellatum''.<ref name=plantlist>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2501530|title=Mollugo verticillata L. — The Plant List|website=www.theplantlist.org|access-date=2016-10-30}}</ref> It is also referred to as alfombra in Spanish and mollugine in French.<ref name=":0">{{ITIS|id=19899|title=''Mollugo verticillata'' L.||access-date=November 3, 2016}}</ref> Other closely related sister taxa include ''Mollugo floriana'', ''Mollugo flavescens'', ''Mollugo snodgrassii'', ''Mollugo crockeri'', and ''Mollugo enneandra''. <ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Christin|first1=Pascal-Antoine|last2=Sage|first2=Tammy L.|last3=Edwards|first3=Erika J.|last4=Ogburn|first4=R. Matthew|last5=Khoshravesh|first5=Roxana|last6=Sage|first6=Rowan F.|date=2011-03-01|title=Complex Evolutionary Transitions and the Significance of C3–C4 Intermediate Forms of Photosynthesis in Molluginaceae|journal=Evolution|language=en|volume=65|issue=3|pages=643–660|doi=10.1111/j.1558-5646.2010.01168.x|pmid=20955197|bibcode=2011Evolu..65..643C |s2cid=41962430|issn=1558-5646}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The wide range of ''M. verticillata'' is apparent across North America, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, West Indies, Central America, South America, Eurasia and Africa.<ref name=idplant>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/163201-2|title=IPNI Plant Name Details|volume=1|website=ipni.org|access-date=2016-10-30}}</ref> There is agreement among some studies that the carpetweed originated in the New World tropics and spread into more temperate zones.<ref name=vert /> Overall the place of origin has been attributed to the tropics or subtropics of the northern and southern hemispheres.<ref name=archeology /> It is commonly found in warm and/or wet environments across North America.<ref name=health />
[[File:Mollugo_verticillata_4035_02.jpg|150px|thumbnail|right|Green carpetweed Molluginaceae Sarsalida Papait ]]

==Uses==
Along with ''Glinus'' (Molluginaceae), ''Mollugo'' are edible plants that have historically been utilized as vegetables or for medicinal benefits.<ref name=family /> The family Molluginaceae has been studied for its therapeutic characteristics due to the production of [[triterpenes]] [[saponin]]s and [[flavonoid]]s{{cn|date=November 2020}}. One study suggested that [[ethanol|ethanolic]] extracts of ''M. verticillata'' could be a potential [[Immunomodulators|immunomodulator]]. The chemical makeup in members of the family Molluginaceae in general has anti-fungal and anti-inflammatory properties.<ref name="health" />

==Ethnobotany==
Carbon dating has dated seeds of ''M. verticillata'' found in [[Icehouse Bottom]] Tennessee back to 1170- 140 B.C. Other seeds found in [[Troyville Earthworks|Troyville]], Louisiana were dated back to 500 A.D. It is unsure exactly when or how ''M. verticillata'' spread into temperate North America. European movements were not the cause of this migration because carbon dating reveals that the plant was in the Little Tennessee river valley 3000 years ago. Despite little apparent  food value, indigenous peoples may have had uses of ''M. verticillata'' that are unclear today. Carpetweed, also referred to as "Indian chickweed", was utilized as a [[Leaf vegetable|potherb]] by the indigenous peoples of Southern Appalachia.<ref name="archeology">{{Cite journal|last1=Chapman|first1=Jefferson|last2=Stewart|first2=Robert|last3=Yarnell|first3=Richard|title=Archaeological Evidence for Precolumbian Introduction of ''Portulaca oleracea'' and ''Mollugo verticillata'' into Eastern North America|journal=Economic Botany|volume=28|issue=4|pages=411–412|doi=10.1007/bf02862857|year=1973|bibcode=1973EcBot..28..411C |s2cid=39745222}}</ref><ref name="aborigines">{{Cite journal|last=Core|first=Earl|date=23 December 1966|title=Ethnobotany of the Southern Appalachian Aborigines|journal=Economic Botany|volume=21|issue=3|pages=199–214|doi=10.1007/BF02860370|s2cid=29029467}}</ref>

==Conservation status==
Carpetweed is considered to be globally secure.<ref name=":1" /> It is also credited as an invasive weed by USDA.gov.<ref name=usda>{{Cite web|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=MOVE|title=Plants Profile for ''Mollugo verticillata'' (green carpetweed)|website=plants.usda.gov|access-date=2016-10-30}}</ref> IUCN RedList states that the taxon has not been assessed for the IUCN Red List. Other accounts cite the weed as being native to the Continental US, Caribbean territories, Mexico and introduced to Canada.<ref name=":0" /> It can be found in disturbed habitats such as fields, parking lots and gardens.<ref name=idplant />
